Que proposent les partis en matière d’ar: What are the parties proposing on firearms?
La question des armes à feu était sur to: Firearms were on the lips of every party leader during this election campaign.
L'arsenal d'un détenteur de permis d'arm: The arsenal of a legal firearms licence holder. Photo: Pablo Ortiz
La question des armes à feu était sur to: Firearms were on the lips of every party leader during this election campaign. What are the parties proposing for better control of these weapons? We broke it down for you. To better understand the issue, it has to be divided into two parts, says Francis Langlois, a specialist in firearms in Canada and the United States: legal firearms and illegal firearms. “These are two issues that call for two different solutions,” he explains. In his view, the public debate on firearms during the election mixed together gun violence in cities and mass shootings. These are two problems that require different solutions, Langlois believes. Illegal firearms: what are the parties proposing to curb this scourge? As for the Green Party, nothing in its platform mentions firearms control. However, party leader Annamie Paul said during the French-language leaders’ debate that the proliferation of firearms has to be tackled at its root. “We know that three-quarters of the weapons used in criminal acts are not attributable to firearms issued with a licence; they come from the black market. So now is the time to tackle the problem at its root, to talk about the upstream problems that can lead to that kind of situation: affordable housing, identity in our society. That’s how you tackle the causes of criminal acts and avoid the overrepresentation of Indigenous peoples and the Black diaspora in our criminal justice system,” we hear her say. The leader did not specify, however, what her community investment plan includes. In an interview with La Converse, the party’s Francophone vice-president, Clément Badra, said he had no information on the party’s proposals regarding border control. On the community prevention plan, he cited the social measures proposed by the party, such as a guaranteed livable income, the abolition of post-secondary tuition fees, universal pharmacare and more accessible mental health care, in order to counter poverty in disadvantaged neighbourhoods. Asked about the budgets allocated to these promises, the Mount Royal candidate gave no details. The Green Party has not costed its promises. As for the NDP, on the issue of firearms smuggling and organized crime, it promises to provide resources and equipment to stem the flow of handguns into the country and to mandate the RCMP to coordinate a firearms trafficking enforcement program. The party told us it wants to give more power to the Canada Border Services Agency, a promise that has not been costed. For the prevention of gun violence, the NDP proposes ensuring that municipalities have access to funding for anti-gang projects in order to deter at-risk youth, by enhancing the programs of the National Crime Prevention Centre. The party says it wants to tackle radicalization by focusing on preventing extremism and violence among youth, notably by supporting community initiatives, a promise that has not yet been costed. Without giving details, the New Democrats denounce the lack of tools to prevent online hate and promise to address it. “The CRTC’s powers could also be strengthened to actively fight this harmful phenomenon,” said Nina Amrov, Jagmeet Singh’s press secretary, in an email. She did not miss the chance to criticize the outgoing government, and did not answer our questions about the budgets allocated to these promises. The Bloc Québécois proposes $100 million a year for federal agencies to combat organized crime and illegal firearms trafficking at the borders. There is no mention of community-based prevention in the Bloc Québécois platform. Asked about this, the party said that social programs fall under provincial jurisdiction and that it wants to increase the Canada Social Transfer (CST) to the provinces by 6% a year. This program targets poverty and social inequality, but does not specifically target marginalized youth. As for the Liberal Party, the outgoing government invested $92.9 million between 2018 and 2025 in the CBSA to counter the illegal entry of firearms. It now proposes strengthening the capacity of the RCMP and the Canada Border Services Agency, a promise that is not costed in the Liberal budget. Asked about this, the Liberal Party had not answered our questions at the time of writing. The outgoing government proposes heavier maximum sentences for firearms trafficking and smuggling, rising from 10 to 14 years of imprisonment. For prevention, it proposes $250 million over five years for municipalities and Indigenous communities to support at-risk youth by investing in activities aimed at stopping the spread of gang-related offences. As for the Conservative Party, it proposes hiring 200 more RCMP officers to fight the smuggling of firearms and drugs, and street gangs. The Conservative Party also proposes heavier sentences for the criminal use of a firearm and the creation of a list of criminal entities. It also proposes amending the firearms legislation to counter straw purchasing, in cases where a firearms licence holder legally buys a weapon and resells it illegally on the black market. To that end, the Conservatives propose amending the Firearms Act so that an individual who transfers a firearm for financial gain on three separate occasions in a calendar year must hold a business licence. Because there is no longer a federal registry for non-restricted weapons, this measure applies only to owners of restricted weapons, that is, handguns and short-barrelled weapons. The Conservative Party also proposes more penalties for offenders. It proposes creating a street gang exit strategy with the private sector to “allow offenders to break free from a cycle of violence and start over in a new place, with a good job and the support needed to leave a life of crime,” a promise that has not been costed. Asked about this, the Conservatives did not answer our questions. Legal firearms: assault weapons control On the issue of legal firearms, the parties in the race propose changes to handguns, assault weapons and licences. What are the parties proposing to control assault weapons? The Bloc Québécois is asking the federal government to amend the Criminal Code to add an “assault weapon” category that would make it possible to ban all military-style semi-automatic long guns. It also wants to invest $900 million to buy back prohibited firearms. “The Liberals are now also promising a mandatory buyback of certain assault weapons, but only for the most popular models, with a budget of $800 million. The Bloc Québécois wants to ban all assault weapons, hence our higher amount,” Bloc Québécois spokesperson Karine Lafontaine explained to La Converse. The Liberal Party is going after high-capacity magazines by requiring that magazines for long guns that can hold more than five cartridges be permanently modified so that they can never hold more than five. It also wants to prohibit the sale or transfer of magazines that could hold more rounds than the legal limit, regardless of how the manufacturer intended them to be used. The outgoing government is proposing tougher assault weapons laws with a mandatory buyback of the assault weapons banned by the May 2020 order in council. The outgoing Liberals banned 1,500 military-style assault weapons, including those used in the Dawson College and Polytechnique shootings. Initially, the Liberal Party did not intend to make the proposed buyback program mandatory; it is due to come into effect next year. If re-elected, the Liberal Party proposes toughening the laws by requiring owners of these firearms to sell them back to the government rather than keep them. As for the NDP, the party promises to “keep assault weapons and handguns off our streets” with a broader definition of prohibited weapons to include new models of assault weapons. It proposes an investment of $500 million for the buyback of assault weapons. On handguns, it proposes allowing municipalities to restrict or ban them. The Green Party does not mention firearms in its platform. Annamie Paul did say during the French-language leaders’ debate, however, that she would ban all handguns and assault weapons. In its platform, the Conservative Party says it wants to repeal the federal Bill C-71, which strengthens firearms legislation, and the May 2020 order in council that bans 1,500 military-style weapons. The party had voted against the 2020 order and unanimously against Bill C-71. During the campaign, however, party leader Erin O’Toole did an about-face and said his government would maintain the restrictions of Bill C-71 and the 2020 order, while conducting a review of the classification system. What are the parties proposing to control handguns? The NDP proposes handing control of handguns over to municipalities. Note that the Liberal Party also proposed passing the responsibility on to municipalities in its Bill C-21 before course-correcting toward the provinces in its election platform. In Quebec, the mayors of Montréal, Québec City, Gatineau, Laval and Longueuil urged the party leaders not to impose responsibility for handgun control on them. The Liberals and the Bloc now both propose passing control of handguns to the provinces. The outgoing government is proposing $1 billion to support the provinces and territories in banning handguns. Several provinces, such as Ontario, Alberta and Saskatchewan, have said they do not want to take on this responsibility. The CAQ government, however, has not taken a clear position on the measure. Asked about it, the office of Public Security Minister Geneviève Guilbault would only say that it will work with whichever federal government is in place on the issue, that it does not want this responsibility to fall to municipalities, and that it will stand up for Quebec’s interests. The Conservative Party promises to “tackle street gang violence that forces too many Canadians to live in fear” without ever mentioning handguns in its election platform. Handguns are the most common type of weapon among street gangs. The party does say, however, that it does not want to harass sport shooters and hunters. Licences and firearms legislation Currently, people must declare for themselves whether they have a history of domestic violence when applying for a firearms licence. Only the Liberals and the Conservatives propose changes to improve licensing laws. The Liberals propose lifetime background checks to prevent people with a history of domestic violence from obtaining a firearms licence. On this point, the Conservatives propose requiring the automatic surrender of firearms if a licence holder is charged with an offence against a person. If the charge is dismissed, the weapon would be returned to the holder. On mental health, the Liberals propose a “red flag” law allowing the immediate confiscation of firearms if a person poses a threat to themselves or others. The Conservative Party instead proposes authorizing a health professional to inform the chief firearms officer if they are treating a person for mental illness and there are reasonable grounds to believe that possessing a firearm could endanger others or the person themselves. The Conservatives go further to protect licence holders, “to ensure that an administrative expiry cannot lead to criminal charges or the seizure of legal firearms owned by a holder.” They also propose making it illegal to acquire new weapons or ammunition before an expired licence is renewed.
<strong>Les mesures de contrôle des arme: Can firearms control measures make the public safer?
Cet été, de nombreuses fusillades ont eu: This summer, there were numerous shootings in neighbourhoods in Montréal, Laval and around the metropolitan area. Gunshots fired in broad daylight and stray bullets have shattered residents’ sense of peace. For a few hundred dollars and without a licence, young people can get their hands on weapons quickly and easily. How do these weapons end up in their hands?
Dans la majorité des cas, ce sont des ar: In the majority of cases, these are illegal weapons brought across the Canada-U.S. border by organized crime. “With one of the longest unfortified borders in the world, there are holes everywhere where trafficking is possible,” explains retired Sûreté du Québec investigator Paul Laurier. “Weapons are very, far too easy to find, and selling weapons is lucrative,” says the former investigator, who worked on organized crime and terrorism. “If Quebec police took away every firearm, I guarantee you that in a month, the weapons would be back.” He links this to the proximity of the U.S. market and the existence of channels between the two countries run by organized crime.
D’après Francis Langlois,chercheur spéci: According to Francis Langlois, a researcher specializing in firearms in Canada and the United States at the Raoul-Dandurand Chair, the American market is too big and U.S. firearms laws are weak. “It’s extremely difficult to counter, and the supply is practically unlimited in the United States. But that’s really where the weapons are found. Our neighbour is the problem,” he says.
Le spécialiste estime cependant que le c: The specialist believes, however, that border control will change nothing about violence in big cities if there is no upstream investment in violence prevention. Former investigator Paul Laurier agrees. “It’s not firearms regulation that’s going to solve the problem. It takes people going out to see young people and to break the cycle,” he says. “If we transform the socio-economic conditions in the neighbourhoods most affected by this violence, young people will be able to find a different path.” “Weapons make this violence deadlier, more dangerous. They don’t necessarily increase crime rates, they multiply the chances of getting killed,” adds Francis Langlois.
La culture des armes à feu témoigne de l: Firearms culture reflects the transformation that has taken place in the industry. “Starting in the 1980s, we ended up with military-style and police-style weapons, semi-automatic weapons,” says Francis Langlois. These weapons were not on the market before. “There is also the spread of the image of the gun as a way to assert your masculinity, to protect yourself. It’s a discourse perpetuated by the industry, and this discourse creates a firearms culture that is more aggressive,” the researcher believes.
On retrouve maintenant sur le marché des: The market now offers semi-automatic pistols that can hold 10, 15 or 20 rounds. Assault rifles can hold up to 100 bullets. Langlois says the Polytechnique massacre would not have been possible without a weapon that could hold 30 projectiles. “There’s a whole rapid-fire shooting discipline, it’s new. It developed in the 1990s and 2000s. They’re not just selling weapons, they’re selling a whole culture.”
« Dans les rues, les tueries, ça ne se p: “On the streets, the shootings don’t happen with long guns. Yes, those cause damage, but the danger is handguns,” says Paul Laurier. Echoing the former investigator, researcher Francis Langlois also argues that the illegal handguns that end up in the hands of street gangs come from the United States. The specialist says he does not understand the emphasis on handgun control in the public debate, since the vast majority of them come from illegal arms trafficking. In his view, then, legal controls will not solve the underlying problem. Some handguns found on the street are nonetheless domestic: they are stolen from the legal market or sold to people without licences by legal licence holders. Nathalie Provost, spokesperson for the organization PolySeSouvient, told us that the number of handguns held by legal owners has doubled in the past ten years. According to Statistics Canada, there are now nearly one million handguns on the legal market.
Plusieurs partis fédéraux se sont pronon: Several federal parties have spoken out on handgun control, passing it on to municipalities or provinces. Francis Langlois and Nathalie Provost both believe that national control is necessary and that these measures are not effective without it. “Even if you ban legal weapons within the City of Montréal, that doesn’t stop weapons from coming into and out of cities,” Langlois believes. He cites the gunman in the 2018 Danforth shooting in Toronto, who obtained his handgun illegally in Toronto. The weapon in question had been sold legally in Saskatchewan.
« Quand on réglemente les armes légales,: “When we regulate legal weapons, it’s mostly to limit mass shootings,” the researcher believes. In his view, the goal of controlling military-style weapons such as assault weapons, which have very great firepower, is tied to public safety in terms of suicides, accidental use and mass shootings. Most of the weapons used in this type of tragedy targeting crowds were purchased legally: this is notably the case for the weapons used at the Québec City mosque and at Dawson College. “These are weapons that are favoured by mass killers. That’s why governments and organizations are seeking to increase control over firearms. They are ideal weapons for soldiers or police officers, but they are not made to be used by civilians,” he says.
Depuis la destruction du registre canadi: Since the destruction of the Canadian firearms registry by the Harper government in 2012, Canada has had no precise data on the number of non-restricted weapons (that is, hunting rifles and long guns) in circulation in the country. It is therefore very difficult to know how many weapons a non-restricted firearms licence holder owns. The Canadian government has thus lost track of many hunting rifles and assault weapons that have been purchased. While the mandatory buyback program proposed by the Liberal Party is interesting in theory, it will be difficult to enforce, the researcher points out.
Comme en témoigne, Charles, un propriéta: Charles, a non-restricted firearms licence holder who does sport shooting, is a case in point. He owns 11 firearms, including 3 assault weapons. None of his weapons is on the 2020 order. The young man has several friends who also own legal firearms. He says the mandatory buyback program mentioned in the May 2020 order has become a “running gag” in the firearms community. “If nobody knows how many people own this type of weapon, there’s an obvious loophole. Who’s going to go tell the government they have one?” he asks.
« Ce que décret permet, c'est que ça met: “What the order does is end the trade in these weapons in Canada. So there's no longer any avenue for legitimate use of them, since it's no longer legal to transport, trade, own or use them. It's not perfect, but if you want to get these weapons off the market, it's a good measure,” the specialist explains. Without a registry for non-restricted firearms, it's hard to legislate, Francis Langlois explains. “It was the best thing we had, we destroyed it, and it's not coming back. It cost too much,” says Nathalie Provost of the firearms registry. The spokesperson for PolySeSouvient believes no party goes far enough to control assault weapons, for fear of losing votes if they propose measures that are too strict on legal firearms.
PolySeSouvient s’indigne de l’argument d: PolySeSouvient is outraged by the Conservatives' argument that they don't want to “blame” gun owners who follow the rules by imposing too many restrictions on legal firearms. “It gives the impression that Trudeau is harassing honest owners, when all he wants is to remove overly powerful weapons. We have nothing against the good owners. We're not taking away their ability to shoot, we're taking away certain models,” says the Polytechnique massacre survivor. She is outraged that a citizen's firepower can be greater than a police officer's.
Madame Provost estime que le gouvernemen: Ms. Provost believes the government should ban all assault weapons, and that they have no place in the hands of citizens. “In every country where there is tighter control of firearms, there are fewer deaths linked to those weapons. I'm not saying it will solve the whole problem of illegal weapons, we're not naive,” she argues. She draws a comparison with vehicles. “Do you realize that a firearm is less controlled than a car? Cars are registered, and all our governments know who has how many cars, how many he has. That's not the case for firearms,” she illustrates. The registry gave law enforcement the information it needed to act.
<strong>Un permis trop facile à obtenir?: Is a licence too easy to get?
« Ce n’est pas difficile d’avoir un perm: “It's not hard to get a firearms licence, but it's very bureaucratic,” Charles tells us. He got his licence in six months. After taking a Canadian Firearms Safety Course, he writes an exam the same day. “Basically, you can't point the gun at the instructor, and you have to show minimal competence in handling firearms,” he says mockingly.
Quelques semaines plus tard. Il reçoit s: A few weeks later, he receives his certificate and can fill out an application for a firearms possession licence on the RCMP website. After a few months, Charles receives a non-restricted firearms licence, which allows him to buy long guns and hunting rifles. No psychological evaluation, no need to justify why he is applying for a firearms licence. “No need to say it's for sport,” he notes. “There are questions about criminal and violent history, but there's nothing on the form about extremist ideologies, and for mental health, it's self-declared,” says the young man.
Le formulaire demande deux références qu: The form asks for two references who vouch for the applicant's ability to obtain a firearms possession and acquisition licence “in the interest of the safety of the applicant or of any other person.” Charles would like more measures to be taken to make sure people who want a firearms licence are of sound mind. He believes the debate doesn't address this aspect enough. “You can always make the licence harder to get, but you have to invest the resources to actually do the checks,” agrees researcher Francis Langlois.
